messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lt. Commander Marcus Collins remembers the hurricane not as a weather event but as a sequence of snapshots that feel both too vivid and not quite real. He was stationed at Naval Air Station Oceana when the storm surge breached the runway and flooded the hangars where dozens of sailors had taken shelter. He can still see the water rising, the metal doors buckling, people scrambling onto lockers and pallet racks. In his mind the pictures are clear—the fluorescent lights flickering, a bottle of rum that smashed against a bulkhead and filled the air with its sharp, sweet smell as the floor tilted. But when he tries to tell the story to his wife, the words feel hollow, as if the event happened to someone else. The memory is so extreme he sometimes catches himself wondering if he dreamed it. And when the images surface—usually without warning—his body locks into that same crouched position, shoulders braced against the cold steel wall, legs numb, the way he was for six hours until the rescue boat came.

The first few weeks after the evacuation, Marcus threw himself into the clean-up. He told himself he had to endure—it was his duty, his fault for not getting everyone out faster. That punishment thinking took root early: *I should have been in the last helicopter, I should have carried more people.* He started working double shifts on debris removal, came home exhausted but unable to sleep. His wife noticed he no longer wanted to go to the grocery store with her; the crowds made his chest tighten. A trip to the base commissary meant passing the same row of buildings where the water had stood, and he would feel his stomach drop, the images flooding back. Even a faint whiff of alcohol—a spilled drink at a cookout, hand sanitizer—could trigger that same metallic taste of panic and the memory of the rum and the screaming.

Over the next months, Marcus’s avoidance hardened into a daily habit. He stopped returning calls from the friends who had been in the hangar with him. Seeing them meant talking about what happened, and talking about it made the story feel even more unreal, more like a movie he couldn't step out of. He also avoided being in the dark—he now sleeps with a nightlight, because darkness pulls him back to that powerless, waiting position. The more he isolated himself, the more he came to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere. He used to think of himself as a happy, gregarious officer, but now he feels set apart from the other service members who seem to have moved on. He is certain they see him as broken. That belief—that he is isolated and lost—sharpens the memories when they come. When he walks into the base gym and sees the corner where the flood line was marked, the narrative of *I don't fit here anymore* makes the images more intense, more bodily. He braces, his shoulders hunch, and the memory feels physically real again.

The cycle turns on itself. The crowding at the weekly command briefings triggers the memory of being packed into that hangar, which makes him feel a fresh wave of misery and estrangement, and that misery in turn makes every crowded corridor or dark stairwell feel like another threat, another reason to get out. He has come to believe that he deserves this suffering, that the nightmares are a fair punishment for surviving when others did not. That punishment thought pushes him to avoid even the simplest circumstances—he takes the long way to his office to avoid the hallway that is too narrow, too dark. Each avoidance strengthens the belief that he cannot handle the world, and each failed attempt to rejoin his old friends confirms that he is indeed a stranger among them.

What finally brought Marcus to the mental health clinic was a single incident on the flight deck last week. A petty officer accidentally bumped into him during a drill, and for a moment Marcus was back in the hangar, crouched against the wall, the smell of rum and seawater in his throat. He shoved the sailor, yelled, and was immediately put on standby. His commanding officer told him to get help or face a fitness report. Marcus is not sure he can change. He is afraid that the story will never feel real, that he will never feel happy again, that the isolation is just what he deserves. But he is also, quietly, tired of the nightlight and the long way to his office.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not demonstrate that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, isolation) cause the patient to perceive new triggers; rather, triggers lead to avoidance, and avoidance reinforces negative appraisals but does not directly create novel triggers.
